BUS.G11.T2.PRESENT.A1.title: Presentation & responding to feedback
BUS.G11.T2.PRESENT.A1.description: Accurate, succinct verbal and non-verbal presentation of business information (tables, graphs, diagrams, posters, handouts), written information such as reports and flyers, and responding to questions and feedback in a non-aggressive, professional manner.
BUS.G11.T2.PRESENT.A1.strand: T2 — Creative thinking, stress & change, action plans, setting up, ethics & presentation
BUS.G11.T2.PRESENT.A1.recovery_strategy: Verbal = spoken/words; non-verbal = visuals (tables, graphs, diagrams). When questioned: answer all questions, make notes, do not argue, and apologise for any errors. Put the most important information first and keep visuals clear.

questions.question: Which of these is a NON-VERBAL way of presenting business information?
questions.expected: A bar graph
questions.memo: Non-verbal presentation uses visuals such as graphs, tables and diagrams; the other options are spoken (verbal).

questions.question: Tables, graphs and diagrams are examples of _________ presentation.
questions.expected: non-verbal
questions.memo: Visual formats such as tables, graphs and diagrams are non-verbal presentation.

questions.question: True or false: A spoken talk to an audience is a verbal presentation.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: A talk uses spoken words, so it is a verbal presentation.

questions.question: Which of these is a visual aid used to support a presentation?
questions.expected: A slide or poster
questions.memo: Slides, posters, charts and handouts are visual aids that support and reinforce a presentation.

questions.question: True or false: A presenter should put the most important information first.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Leading with the most important information makes sure the audience gets the key message even if time runs short.

questions.question: When answering a question about your presentation, you should NOT _________.
questions.expected: argue
questions.memo: You should answer questions calmly and professionally — not argue with the person asking.

questions.question: Sort each format into verbal or non-verbal presentation.
questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Spoken formats (talk, reading aloud, answering) are verbal; visual formats (charts, diagrams, tables) are non-verbal.

questions.question: An audience member challenges a figure in your presentation. What is the most professional response?
options: Answer calmly, make a note of it, and check the figure if unsure
Argue loudly that you are right
questions.expected: Answer calmly, make a note of it, and check the figure if unsure
questions.memo: Responding professionally means staying calm, noting the point, and checking facts rather than arguing.

questions.question: Put the steps of preparing a presentation in a sensible order.

items.text: Identify the audience and the key message
Design clear visual aids to support it

questions.expected: audience, content, aids, rehearse
questions.memo: Know your audience and message, organise the content, design the visuals, then rehearse — that order builds a strong presentation.

questions.question: A written summary handed to the audience to support a talk is called a _________.
questions.expected: handout
questions.memo: A handout is a printed summary given to the audience to reinforce the spoken message.

questions.question: Why should visual aids be kept clear and simple?
options: So the audience can understand the message quickly
So the slides take longer to read
So less information is ever shared
questions.expected: So the audience can understand the message quickly
questions.memo: Clear, simple visuals help the audience grasp the message fast, rather than struggling with clutter.

questions.question: True or false: If you realise you made an error in your presentation, you should apologise and correct it.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Professionals acknowledge mistakes, apologise and put them right, which keeps the audience's trust.

questions.question: Sort each response to audience feedback into professional or unprofessional.

items.text: Mocking someone for asking a question
Apologising for and fixing an error

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Professional: answer politely, note feedback, fix errors. Unprofessional: arguing, mocking, or refusing to respond.

questions.question: What is the purpose of support materials such as slides and handouts?
options: To reinforce and clarify the spoken message
To make the talk longer for no reason
questions.expected: To reinforce and clarify the spoken message
questions.memo: Support materials back up the spoken presentation, helping the audience follow and remember the message.

questions.question: A good business report should include _________.
options: clear headings and supporting tables or graphs
questions.expected: clear headings and supporting tables or graphs
questions.memo: A clear report uses headings and visual support (tables, graphs) so readers can follow the information easily.

questions.question: Put the steps of writing a business report in a sensible order.

items.text: Decide the purpose and reader of the report
Draft the report with clear headings

questions.expected: purpose, gather, draft, review
questions.memo: Decide the purpose and reader, gather information, draft with clear headings, then review and finalise.

questions.question: A questioner is hostile and tries to provoke you during a presentation. What is the best response?
options: Stay calm, answer the point factually, and keep your composure
Shout back to show you are in charge
questions.expected: Stay calm, answer the point factually, and keep your composure
questions.memo: Staying calm and answering factually keeps you professional and credible, even when a questioner is difficult.

questions.question: A presenter argues with every audience member who gives feedback. Why does this harm the presentation?
options: It looks unprofessional and discourages useful feedback
It makes the presenter more credible
It improves the quality of the slides
It shortens the question time helpfully
questions.expected: It looks unprofessional and discourages useful feedback
questions.memo: Arguing with feedback appears defensive and unprofessional, and it stops people offering the useful comments that could improve the work.

questions.question: Why can a well-chosen graph communicate some information better than words alone?
options: It shows patterns and comparisons at a glance
It hides the data from the audience
It removes the need for any explanation ever
questions.expected: It shows patterns and comparisons at a glance
questions.memo: A graph makes trends and comparisons visible instantly, which words alone often cannot do as quickly.

questions.question: After a presentation, several people point out the same weakness. What should the presenter do?
options: Take the feedback on board and amend the presentation for next time
Ignore it because the presentation is finished
Delete the presentation and give up
questions.expected: Take the feedback on board and amend the presentation for next time
questions.memo: Consistent feedback signals a real weakness; a professional uses it to amend and improve future presentations.
